statement: In an online panel of US adults matched to the population on sex, age and ethnicity only (Prolific, October 2021; Simonsson et al., 2023), 613 of 2,822 respondents (21.7%) had ever used a classic psychedelic (LSD, psilocybin, ayahuasca, DMT, mescaline, peyote or San Pedro). Asked once, looking back over their whole life, 362 of the 613 (59.1%) said they had never had a challenging, difficult or distressing experience with them, 143 (23.3%) rarely, 80 (13.1%) occasionally and 28 (4.6%) regularly or frequently: 41 in 100 at least once (editors' calculation). 28 (4.6%) said their ability to function had been severely impaired, and 55 (9.0%; printed 8.9%) that impairment had lasted more than a day, 21 of them (3.4%) more than a month (editors' sum), but the two impairment questions gave counts that do not agree (176 reported some impairment, 262 gave its length). All 613, including the 362 who said they had never had one, were asked about their most challenging experience; in the days or weeks after it, 41 (6.7%) reported thoughts or attempts to hurt themselves or others, including 9 (1.5%) attempts to harm themselves, and 16 (2.6%) sought medical, psychiatric or psychological help. 350 (57.1%) reported at least one symptom lasting at least a few days that they put down to psychedelics, most often feeling anxious (36.1%) or difficulty sleeping (27.9%), but these questions, borrowed from meditation research, were not asked of people who had not used psychedelics or about times without them, so how many such symptoms would have happened anyway is unknown; 482 (78.6%) agreed, at least slightly, that they were glad to have used psychedelics. Challenging experiences were linked most often to LSD (by 31.5% of those who had used it, against 19.7% for psilocybin, ayahuasca or DMT and 14.7% for mescaline, peyote or San Pedro), but how often each drug had been used was not asked. The 8 people taking lithium and the 16 taking another mood stabilizer at the time of their most challenging experience had higher odds of later harm thoughts or attempts (odds ratios 22.34, 95% CI 1.78 to 279.65, and 5.84, 1.40 to 24.34, adjusted only for the other medicines), estimates too imprecise, and too open to confounding by the conditions these medicines treat, to give a risk. In a self-selected online sample of people who had used psychedelics, 555 of 869 (64 in 100) said the experience they described had included a period of distress, difficulty or discomfort (Wood et al., 2024), a reminder that such figures depend on who is asked and how. In a prospective study that measured well-being before and after a planned psychedelic experience (Haijen et al., 2018), 85 of the 279 people who answered both surveys (30 in 100, editors' calculation) scored lower two weeks later, counting any fall however small, and they had not rated the experience as more challenging than the others (the paper gives no statistics for this comparison); many who started did not answer the later surveys, and with no comparison group the fall cannot be put down to the drug. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In one US online survey, 59 in 100 people who had ever used a psychedelic said they had never had a difficult experience, and 41 in 100 had had at least one. About 5 in 100 said one had badly affected their daily life, 7 in 100 thought about or tried hurting themselves or others in the days or weeks after, and 3 in 100 got help. Many said worry or poor sleep lasted days, but nobody who had not used psychedelics was asked the same questions, so it is not known how many of these problems would have happened anyway.
population: Adults in the United States who had ever used a classic psychedelic, in an opt-in online panel matched on sex, age and ethnicity (613 of 2,822), with a self-selected online sample and one prospective cohort for comparison
exposure: Lifetime use of classic psychedelics (LSD, psilocybin, ayahuasca, DMT, mescaline, peyote, San Pedro)
comparator: None for the frequencies (no group without psychedelic use answered the same questions)
outcome: Challenging, difficult or distressing experiences; impaired functioning and its length; symptoms lasting days that respondents attributed to psychedelics; thoughts or attempts to hurt oneself or others; help-seeking
magnitude: Simonsson et al. (2023), of 613: never had a challenging experience 362 (59.1%); at least once 251 (40.9%, editors'); severe impairment 28 (4.6%); impairment over a day 55 (9.0%), over a month 21 (3.4%, editors'); harm thoughts or attempts 41 (6.7%), self-harm attempts 9 (1.5%); sought help 16 (2.6%); lasting symptoms attributed to psychedelics 350 (57.1%, no comparison group); glad 482 (78.6%, slightly to strongly agree). Lithium (8 people) OR 22.34 (1.78 to 279.65), other mood stabilizers (16) 5.84 (1.40 to 24.34), adjusted only for the other medicines. Wood et al. (2024): 555 of 869 (63.9%) recalled distress in the experience they described. Haijen et al. (2018): well-being lower at two weeks (any fall) in 85 of the 279 with both measurements (30.5%).

risk_of_bias.note: Measurement: one retrospective lifetime question; impairment items borrowed from meditation research gave counts that do not agree; the lasting-symptom items have no comparison group (card sc_simonsson_2023).

inconsistency.note: The self-selected survey's higher figure (64 in 100) asked a different question of a different sample; reported as such, not pooled.

indirectness.note: Coverage: an opt-in commercial panel matched on three characteristics only, in one country in 2021, called nationally representative by its authors; the share of the panel who had ever used a psychedelic was higher than the authors had expected from national data when they planned the sample (card sc_simonsson_2023, selection effects).

imprecision.note: 613 people; the rarer figures are stated as counts with their denominators.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim, rated as a description of the population sampled: starts low; down one for measurement (risk of bias) and one for coverage (indirectness), giving very low; never upgraded. Status single study: the frequencies come from one survey; the self-selected survey and the prospective cohort are reported as context, not as replication. The lithium and mood-stabilizer associations rest on 8 and 16 people and are confounded by indication: a signal, not an estimate.

Review and adjudication, before-and-during round: AI reader 280 (adjudicator) re-read Simonsson et al. in full on PMC (no saved copy existed) and checked the second readers' notes. 'Glad' now says agreed at least slightly (142 of the 482 slightly agreed); the lithium and mood-stabilizer odds ratios are marked as adjusted only for the other medicines (Table 4 note; no other covariates); the statement now says that all 613, including the 362 who reported no challenging experience, answered the most-challenging-experience questions; Wood's figure is called a reminder rather than a demonstration. Haijen: 'the one study' removed; the 85 of 279 are those who answered both surveys, a fall is any fall, the paper gives no statistics for the comparison of challenge ratings, and many who started did not answer later surveys. Indirectness note: the panel's share of people who had ever used a psychedelic exceeded the authors' planning estimate (card). Certainty and status unchanged.
Anchor labels: the blind second reader who matched each anchor is named (was 'AI reader 2').
